extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media students, and journalism researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A catalog of criteria (news values) editors and journalists use to decide which events become published news and how they are presented. Includes classical factors (Galtung & Ruge), contemporary updates (Harcup & O'Neill), process-oriented values, audience-perception considerations, and methodological approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that occur suddenly and fit well with the news organization's schedule are more likely to be reported than those that occur gradually or at inconvenient times of day or night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term trends are less likely to receive coverage; items that align with editorial production cycles get selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that have only just happened, are current, ongoing, or are about to happen are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediacy increases selection probability; ties into deadlines and the value of freshness for audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity / Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories to do with people or places close to the target audience (geographical and cultural proximity) are more likely to be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called 'proximity' or 'meaningfulness'—events that audiences can readily understand or identify with receive priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news is more newsworthy than good news; often described as 'the basic news value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes disasters, crime, and adverse developments; tends to drive placement and repeated coverage, though some genres/contexts value positivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive or 'good' news can be a distinct news value in contexts such as sports, science, or feel-good tabloid stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harcup & O'Neill highlighted that good news can be newsworthy and interacts with other values like shareability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition of people or forces resulting in a dramatic effect; fights between individuals, groups, or nations are more likely to be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict often leads to extended coverage and updates; in politics it enables persuasive framing and increased audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are out of the ordinary, unexpected, or rare are more newsworthy than routine, unsurprising events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising elements attract attention; tension exists with consonance (what media expect and are ready to cover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events whose implications are clear make for better copy than those open to multiple interpretations or requiring complex background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear-cut stories are preferred because they are easier to report and understand rapidly; ambiguous events may be de-prioritized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that can be portrayed as the actions of individuals are more attractive than those without identifiable human agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization helps contextualize topics in human terms and supports human-interest angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Relates to the audience's sense of identification with a topic; cultural proximity (shared language, appearance, preoccupations) increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely linked with relevance—if audiences see themselves reflected, coverage likelihood increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: How relevant the event is to the target readers/viewers' own lives or experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance can be manipulated by communicators; editors judge whether a story crosses the audience's 'boundary of relevance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: An event's significance or consequences for the target audience or others—events with significant consequences are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact refers both to event impact (who is affected) and story impact (reach/engagement once published).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events concerned with global powers, the rich, powerful, famous and infamous receive more attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes eliteness of sources (attribution); prominence of actors interacts with other values like conflict and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving popular political leaders, celebrities, or influential organizations are more likely to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern news increasingly focuses on well-known figures; prominence amplifies audience recognition and attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events with a large scale, scope, or high intensity are more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of extremes (largest, worst, best) increases editorial salience; overlaps with impact and eliteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that fit with the media's expectations and preconceptions receive more coverage than those that defy them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consonance refers to editorial readiness, stereotypes, and mental scripts; it can conflict with unexpectedness but explains why familiar story-types are fast-covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A story already in the news gathers inertia—previous coverage makes it easier to follow and update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing items benefit from established resources and audience familiarity; continuity shapes editorial agendas and follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must compete with each other for space; editors seek balance across types of coverage and may demote stories to maintain variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominence given to a story depends both on its own news values and the values of competing stories in the same edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or professional competition between media can lead journalists to endorse or follow another outlet's news valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rival coverage can elevate items; chasing competitors influences speed and topic selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-option
rubrics_metrics.description: A story marginally newsworthy in itself may be covered if related to a major ongoing story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may link minor items to 'big' narratives to justify coverage (e.g., side-stories attached to a running theme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: A marginal story that is already written and available may be selected ahead of a more newsworthy item that requires original reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readily available copy (press releases, pre-written pieces) can displace items needing fieldwork; logistical convenience matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-scheduled events (e.g., elections, sports fixtures) are more likely to be covered because they are planned and anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictable events allow resource planning and preparation, increasing coverage probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story impact / Shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of a published story—whether it is widely shared, read, liked, commented on—now influences selection and prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareability favors simple, emotional, unexpected, and triggered content; digital analytics (clicks, shares) increasingly shape newsroom priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional media formats with strict deadlines and short production cycles select for items that can be researched and covered quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines favor stories that are fast to verify and produce; time pressure affects both selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to deploy and control reporting staff and technical resources affects whether remote or complex stories are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications, transport, safety, and equipment constraints can preclude coverage despite newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data / Facticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Media need to back up stories with data to remain relevant and reliable; reporters prefer raw data for unbiased perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called 'facticity'—stories supported by verifiable facts and figures are favored in hard news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain of news communication (selection, distortion, replication) and selection hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge's model: selection (events satisfying more factors are likelier to be selected), distortion (accentuating newsworthy factors), and replication (these processes repeat through the production chain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes additivity hypothesis (more factors → higher probability), complementary hypothesis (factors tend to exclude each other), and exclusion hypothesis (events satisfying few/no factors won't become news).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological perspectives on news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Four approaches to studying news values: material (material reality of events), cognitive (people's beliefs/value systems), social (journalistic practice), and discursive (how words/images construct newsworthiness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discursive perspective leads to methods like Discursive News Values Analysis (DNVA) which examine how negativity, proximity, eliteness, etc., are constructed in published stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discursive News Values Analysis (DNVA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical method influenced by linguistics and social semiotics that examines how news values are constructed through language and images in published stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on the 'distortion' step—how events are discursively framed as newsworthy; useful for understanding rhetorical and visual tactics that signal newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience perception: Risk signals / Security concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences attend to information that signals threats to peace, prosperity, or well-being; newsworthiness can be framed as a 'risk signal' combining change and relevance to security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and publicists may manipulate perceived change and relevance to amplify or downplay a story's risk signal; relevance declines past a 'boundary of relevance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Political usefulness bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions of newsworthiness can be contaminated by political usefulness—people deem stories more newsworthy if they provide 'ammunition' for their political views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bias affects audience judgement and can feed back into editorial decisions when audience input is solicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary / psychological explanations (negativity bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human perceptual systems react faster to negative stimuli, making negative news more attention-grabbing and memorable; this helps explain media preference for negative stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains gendered differences claimed in reception and framing, but scholars urge caution about overgeneralizing evolutionary accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary digital metrics: immediacy and shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: In the digital era, factors such as shareability and immediacy increasingly determine what gets reported—stories likely to generate clicks and social engagement may receive more attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional values (conflict, prominence) remain relevant but interact with analytics-driven priorities; audience feedback and platform algorithms shape editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill contemporary additions (celebrity, good news, newspaper agenda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Updates to classical lists: rise of celebrity news, inclusion of good news as a distinct value in some contexts, and the influence of a publication's own agenda on selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that news values evolve; organizational priorities and market pressures shape what counts as news in practice.
